item.title: The Art of Not Making an AI Safety Deal With China
item.description: Silicon Valley leaders keep painting artificial intelligence doomsday scenarios, yet they also can’t stop racing to build and sell it. They often point to China as the reason they have no choice, even as the post-ChatGPT era suggests the fiercest pressure comes from one another.
item.dc:creator: Catherine Thorbecke

item.title: Tokyo, Japan's Shibuya Is Changing. I Hope It Never Stops
item.description: A $14 billion construction project is being accused of costing Shibuya its soul. That gets it backward.
item.dc:creator: Gearoid Reidy

item.title: Japan's GPIF Pension Fund Needs a CalPERS Lesson
item.description: Traders closely study how pensions funds, controlling $73 trillion, plan to spend their firepower. But lately, the industry’s biggest whales are creating outsized dislocation and trepidation in global currency and bond markets. The excessive market scrutiny and speculation that big pension funds are attracting now demands a rethink in portfolio management.
item.dc:creator: Shuli Ren

item.title: AAA AI
item.description: AI lab ratings, hourly levered ETFs, Treasury selling Treasury futures and egg fines.
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine

item.title: Bond Traders Shrug Off Bessent’s Buyback Gimmick
item.description: Well, that didn’t go as planned. When the Treasury Department announced three weeks ago that it would increase buybacks of longer-term US government bonds “by at least double,” it described the plan as a form of “liquidity support.”
item.dc:creator: Robert Burgess

item.title: New Hampshire: Sununu Helps Republicans’ Fight to Keep the Senate
item.description: The Democratic Party’s bid to wrest control of the US Senate in the upcoming midterm elections faces a fresh hurdle in battleground New Hampshire after Republicans nominated John E. Sununu, a Capitol Hill veteran with a popular family name.
item.dc:creator: David M. Drucker

item.title: Republican Dallas Convention Is a Big, Risky Bet on Trump
item.description: President Donald Trump remains the GOP’s biggest draw. But, with his record low approval ratings, he is also the GOP’s biggest liability. That’s the tightrope Republicans face as they kick off their first-ever midterm convention, further nationalizing a race that is already set to be a referendum on Trump. It’s a high-risk, possibly high-reward gamble.
item.dc:creator: Nia-Malika Henderson

item.title: Carney, Canada and Europe Are Building a Hedge Against America and Trump
item.description: Is Canada becoming the European Union’s 28th state, rather than America’s 51st? Next week, Prime Minister Mark Carney will join EU President Ursula von der Leyen in announcing a plan for deeper ties as the Trump administration escalates its trade war against its neighbor. Closer trade, security, supply chains and critical raw materials are all on the table for allies looking to offset a wayward US hegemon.
item.dc:creator: Lionel Laurent

item.title: Bank Resolution Regimes Need Urgent Reform to Protect Financial Stability
item.description: How to resolve a failed bank may seem like an arcane subject. Nevertheless, as demonstrated during the banking turmoil of 2023, it has important implications for financial stability, taxpayers, and trust in the financial system. The failure of the parent to Silicon Valley Bank resulted in almost $20 billion of losses for the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. item.dc:creator: Bill Dudley

item.title: Brazil’s Supreme Court Is Betraying Its Citizens
item.description: Brasilia is finally getting rain, ending a punishing dry season. Inside the government’s iconic modernist buildings, though, the temperature is only rising.
item.dc:creator: Juan Pablo Spinetto

item.title: The Case Against Cutting Social Security Benefits
item.description: Are Social Security benefits too generous? Some fiscal hawks and classic conservatives say the answer is yes, and see the upcoming depletion of the trust fund as an opportunity to rein them in. Social Security was meant to be insurance against poverty, they say, not the sole source of income for a middle-class retirement. The program needs to institute benefit caps, means testing, or even a flat benefit to remain viable.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Anne Edwards

item.title: Medicare Spending Should Have Bond Traders On High Alert
item.description: Anyone concerned about the nation’s $40 trillion debt burden ought to take a hard look at Medicare. Over the next decade, the health program for the elderly will account for more than half of government borrowing, up from about a third today.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: A $2,000 iPhone Gives New Apple CEO John Ternus His Steve Jobs Moment
item.description: When John Ternus succeeded Tim Cook as chief executive officer of Apple Inc. at the start of this month, he needed no introduction to the company’s more than 160,000 employees. The same can’t really be said of the public, most of whom will be meeting, and sizing up, Apple’s new top boss for the first time on Wednesday. He’ll begin by making the case for buying an iPhone that costs at least $2,000.
item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: The Fed’s Three Choices as Warsh’s Honeymoon Ends
item.description: With a week until a key Federal Reserve meeting, President Donald Trump has lobbed his first threat at Kevin Warsh, the new chair he put on the job. “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart — BE PATRIOTS for a change,” he posted Friday, urging policymakers to cut interest rates even as the market sees better-than-even odds of a hike to counter inflation. Trump added: “High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!”
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: UK Politics: Andy Burnham’s Signature Devolution Policy May Be His Undoing
item.description: The one thing we know about Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, other than that he’s from the north, is that he wants to devolve more power to local government. On everything else he has been vague. Public ownership of utilities? The details are in the post. A closer relationship with the European Union? item.dc:creator: Adrian Wooldridge

item.title: Rising Yen Finally Gets Some Respect
item.description: The rest of the world may need to learn to do without cheap Japanese funding.
item.dc:creator: John Authers

item.title: Farage's Rule-Breaking Is a Feature of Reform, Not a Bug
item.description: When Nigel Farage returned to the House of Commons after triggering an unnecessary by-election this summer, he marked the occasion with a video filmed from Parliament’s rooftop. The honey-hued stonework of the Palace of Westminster, set against a clear blue sky, created a fabulous social-media backdrop. Unfortunately, for safety and security reasons, filming on Parliament’s roof is strictly forbidden — as anyone who’s worked on the estate knows. The authorities duly reprimanded Farage.
item.dc:creator: Rosa Prince
